title: Selling It - by Seth Glickman - HEALTH CARE un-covered
description:
Why this one matters I’m a physician and a former health care executive, and I write about the incentives inside for-profit insurance and hospitals.
The same issue carried an article, “Give Your Medicare Plan a Checkup,” that laid out those tradeoffs fairly.
What Chapter is Chapter is a trade name for Memoir, Inc., a privately held company whose subsidiary, Chapter Advisory, LLC, is a licensed health insurance agency.
Chapter doesn’t hide this.
CR doesn’t recommend a car without testing it, and it should hold this partnership to the same standard.
text:
When I was growing up, Consumer Reports was in nearly every room of our house. My parents, both academics, loved bringing evidence to everyday decisions, and on a tight budget, CR helped them save where they could.

I read every issue cover to cover, starting at the back, where “Selling It” featured misleading and absurd marketing claims sent in by readers: a running belt with a slot for a pack of cigarettes, packages that kept their size and price while the product inside quietly shrank. “Selling It” worked because CR was trusted and had no stake in the products it was poking fun at.

CR retired the feature a few years ago. I’m still a member, though now I start at the front.

So when I turned over the latest issue, for a moment I thought “Selling It” was back. The entire back cover was a single ad. In large green letters: “Get Unbiased Medicare Advice.” Below that, CR said it had “teamed up with Chapter” to offer members free, personalized support from “licensed Medicare Advisors.”

But there was no “Selling It” banner. This was CR’s own ad, from the very magazine that taught me to read marketing claims like this with a critical eye.

Why this one matters

I’m a physician and a former health care executive, and I write about the incentives inside for-profit insurance and hospitals. Choosing between Original Medicare (with or without a Medigap plan) and a private Medicare Advantage plan is one of the most consequential decisions an older adult makes. It shapes which doctors you can see, which treatments need an insurer’s approval, and what you could owe in a bad year. It is also hard to reverse, because in most states Medigap insurers can deny coverage or charge more after the initial enrollment window.

The same issue carried an article, “Give Your Medicare Plan a Checkup,” that laid out those tradeoffs fairly. Then the back cover sent readers to a company with a direct financial stake in the outcome.

CR prides itself on being “independent and nonprofit,” with a mission “to create a fair and just marketplace for all.” The back cover doesn’t tell members what Chapter is, how it makes money, or whether CR is paid for the referral. So I went to Chapter’s website.

What Chapter is

Chapter is a trade name for Memoir, Inc., a privately held company whose subsidiary, Chapter Advisory, LLC, is a licensed health insurance agency. In plain terms, the “licensed Medicare Advisors” in the ad are licensed insurance agents. There is no separate license for giving Medicare advice.

Chapter doesn’t hide this. The fine print on its landing page for CR members says it “may receive compensation from an insurance carrier when you enroll in a plan,” represents 50 insurance organizations, and does not offer every plan in every area. None of that made it onto the back cover.

Chapter is also venture-backed. Vivek Ramaswamy is a co-founder. Its 2021 Series A was led by Narya Capital, J.D. Vance’s venture firm, and by Peter Thiel. Vance, and later Thiel, served on Chapter’s board before stepping down. In April 2026 the company raised another $100 million, saying its valuation had more than doubled from $1.5 billion a year earlier and its annual recurring revenue had passed $100 million.

I’m not raising the investors to make a political point, but because they tell you what kind of company this is. Venture investors expect large returns quickly, and an insurance agency’s revenue comes from insurers.

Follow the money

Insurers pay agents and brokers to enroll people in their plans. A study published in May in JAMA Internal Medicine estimated that Medicare Advantage broker payments grew from about $3.9 billion in 2014 to roughly $10 billion in 2022. About three-quarters came from renewals, annual payments that continue for as long as the person stays in the plan.

Concern about these payments crosses party lines. In June, a brief from Republicans on Congress’s Joint Economic Committee found that annual broker spending across Medicare Advantage, Part D, and the ACA markets exceeds $25 billion. In 2023, Medicare Advantage insurers spent an average of $234 per member on brokers, more than they spent on vision, hearing, or dental benefits.

In fairness, agents also earn commissions on Medigap policies, and Chapter says it advises people choosing Original Medicare too. The issue isn’t any single recommendation. It’s that the business runs on payments from insurers, and the person relying on the advice usually doesn’t see how that shapes it.

“Unbiased” according to whom?

Chapter’s answer is that its advisors are paid the same regardless of plan, and that it will recommend plans it doesn’t sell. In 2023 testimony to the Senate Finance Committee, Chapter noted that brokers have no legal obligation to put beneficiaries’ interests first and said it supports a higher standard. Plan-neutral pay for advisors is better than the alternative.

But advisor pay is only one piece of what shapes the advice. It doesn’t tell you:

Which insurers Chapter contracts with where you live, and which it doesn’t.

How much the company earns from each insurer, including renewals and any bonuses or marketing payments.

How its software ranks plans, and what its advisors are trained to say.

How advisors are evaluated: by enrollments, call volume, or something else.

Whether CR is paid for sending members to Chapter. At least one other Chapter referral partner discloses that it may receive a referral fee. CR’s materials say nothing either way.

Chapter’s own page for CR members describes the company as “an independent Medicare advisor.” The word “unbiased” appears only on CR’s back cover, with CR’s name behind it.

Share

That word carries weight in this market. In May 2025, the Justice Department joined a whistleblower lawsuit alleging that Aetna, Elevance Health, and Humana paid hundreds of millions of dollars in kickbacks, labeled as marketing payments, to three of the largest Medicare brokers, eHealth, GoHealth, and SelectQuote, to steer people into their plans. One broker had assured customers its advisors would find the right plan “no matter the carrier.” In March, a federal judge declined to dismiss the core claims. The companies deny wrongdoing, and the case has not been decided. Chapter is not a party and has not been accused of wrongdoing, but the case shows why “unbiased” is a claim that calls for evidence.

The other side of the scale

Now consider who helps people understand Original Medicare: mostly the State Health Insurance Assistance Programs, or SHIPs, which offer free counseling in every state. Their federal funding this year is about $90 million, and nearly half of their roughly 10,000 staff and volunteers are unpaid. Nonprofits like the Medicare Rights Center and the Center for Medicare Advocacy help too. None of them earns anything based on what plan people choose. With $90 million on one side and roughly $10 billion a year in broker payments on the other, it’s not a level playing field.

Regulation is moving the wrong way

Regulators have tried to rein in these incentives. In 2024, CMS capped total payments to agents and brokers, but a federal court in Texas vacated the compensation provisions in August 2025, finding that CMS had exceeded its authority. Then, in its rule for 2027 plans, CMS loosened several marketing protections effective October 1, 2026, including eliminating the 48-hour waiting period before a sales appointment.

Open enrollment runs from October 15 through December 7. This year, older adults will choose Medicare options with fewer guardrails, more marketing, and, in CR’s case, a trusted name behind the pitch. CR isn’t alone. Other prominent organizations, such as the National Council on Aging, have partnered with Chapter. When respected nonprofits lend their credibility to a commission-based business, members deserve to know the terms.

What should happen now

CR should show its work. CR doesn’t recommend a car without testing it, and it should hold this partnership to the same standard. That means disclosing whether Chapter pays CR, explaining the diligence behind the word “unbiased,” and publishing outcomes for members who used the service: how many chose Medicare Advantage versus Original Medicare with Medigap, which insurers they chose, how often they enrolled in plans Chapter doesn’t sell, and how many switched within two years. If the advice is plan-neutral, the data should show it. Until then, CR should stop calling the service “unbiased.”

Chapter should make its disclosure meaningful. It should explain how its compensation varies across the plans it recommends, at the point of advice and in plain terms. Referring organizations like CR are best positioned to judge whether that disclosure is sufficient and should require it as a condition of the relationship.

Policymakers should close the gaps. Since the courts have said CMS lacks the authority to set broker pay, Congress should require disclosure of insurer payments when advice is given, establish a duty to act in the person’s best interest, and limit the use of words like “unbiased” and “independent” by companies paid by the insurers they recommend.

Older adults need better tools and better-funded help. Funding for SHIPs and nonprofit advocates should reflect the importance of the decisions they support. People also need decision tools built by organizations with no financial stake, putting Original Medicare with Medigap on equal footing with Medicare Advantage and showing how each option would work with a person’s own doctors, medications, and budget.

If “Selling It” were still running, I’d send this one in myself. Consumer Reports taught me, and generations of readers, to look past the label and ask who benefits. That lesson applies to its own back cover. I’m still a member, and I’d like to trust what I read, front cover to back.

title: Kroger and Albertsons: the food fight every dealmaker should be watching | Fortune
description:
But when supermarket giant Kroger agreed to acquire Albertsons for $24.6 billion in 2022, a pledge to try was not enough.
In a form of commitment that amounts to what the lawyers call “hell or high water,” Kroger agreed to take “any and all actions” necessary to win approval.
Albertsons terminated the deal and sued Kroger the next day.
I can only assume the Albertsons team was dumbstruck to discover that, when the water rose, Kroger bailed.
Even former Kroger CEO Rodney McMullen has conceded under oath that Kroger had agreed to do whatever the contract required.
text:
But when supermarket giant Kroger agreed to acquire Albertsons for $24.6 billion in 2022, a pledge to try was not enough. In a form of commitment that amounts to what the lawyers call “hell or high water,” Kroger agreed to take “any and all actions” necessary to win approval. That is a big burden, which was understandably interpreted by Albertsons as a clear signal that Kroger was committed to honoring its contract and was all in on the deal.

Then the high water arrived. In December 2024, on the same day, a federal judge in Oregon granted the Federal Trade Commission’s request to block the merger and a state judge in Seattle did the same in a suit brought by Washington’s Attorney General. Albertsons terminated the deal and sued Kroger the next day.

I can only assume the Albertsons team was dumbstruck to discover that, when the water rose, Kroger bailed.

This week, the Delaware Court of Chancery began hearing from the formidable legal teams both grocery giants have fielded, and will ultimately have to decide whether Kroger did indeed do everything it could to honor its contract. Both sides’ pre-trial briefings show the roadmaps they will each follow over the course of the two-week trial to make their respective cases. Quite frankly, based on those detailed documents, it does not look good for team Kroger.

If Albertsons succeeds, the resulting damage award Kroger must pay could prove to be significant. According to the plaintiff’s calculations, an award could be more than $8 billion – which is ironic considering Albertsons will argue that Kroger prioritized its financial return over its obligations. This is a case every dealmaker in America will be watching closely, both because of the money involved but also because the court might better define what the words “any and all actions” really mean.

A review of what has been filed suggests that Kroger’s argument will be that it really, really, really tried. The company spent heavily pursuing approval and had every economic incentive to close, but the Biden administration’s skeptical regulators were just never satisfied that the company’s proposed plans would protect competition and consumers. You cannot bill us for the politically motivated actions of others, Kroger will say.

The problem, says Albertsons, is that the contract is clear. Trying hard is not enough to fulfill what the contract requires. Even former Kroger CEO Rodney McMullen has conceded under oath that Kroger had agreed to do whatever the contract required.

When attorneys transact a merger between two retail giants like Albertsons and Kroger, a standard strategy to address anticompetitive concerns is to spin off a new competitor. But the spin off must be truly able to compete. It is not just a matter of selling off a certain number of stores, a selection of private label products, manufacturing sites, and other assets. You must offload the right stores and the right assets to build a viable business that shoppers will consider.

Albertsons will argue that Kroger did not even try. Instead of deciding what to sell off to create a new competitor, Kroger focused on what stores and assets it would never sell. In other words, the merged company would hold on to Kroger’s crown jewels, and any new firm would get the leftovers. As a result, the courts and the FTC both decided that the new competition would be inadequate.

Indeed, Kroger allegedly baked the resistance into the pay packages granted to its top leaders. Senior executives stood to collect bonuses worth as much as six times their base salaries if the merger closed while delivering Kroger’s targeted financial returns. That incentivized those bosses to resist selling more valuable stores or other assets, even if it cost them the deal.

Then there are the departures the lawyers on both sides seem eager to avoid explaining. McMullen, who was Kroger’s Chairman and CEO through most of the approval fight, and his CFO Gary Millerchip left the company at crucial moments in the process. McMullen’s departure was blamed on unspecified personal behavior issues. Millerchip’s was tied to a lucrative new job at Costco.

To this day, the actual reason for McMullen’s departure remains shrouded in secrecy.

But all of this should not obscure what the Delaware court is being asked to decide.

This is not, at its core, a referendum on McMullen’s character, Kroger’s corporate culture, the alleged avarice of its senior leaders, or even the company’s allegedly poor divestiture process. It is a contract case.

Kroger made a specific, unusually demanding promise that it would take “any and all actions” necessary to get the merger approved. Albertsons says when the necessary actions became too expensive – when Kroger figured out it would have to sell stores and assets it wanted to keep – Kroger called it quits.

That is the whole dispute. Kroger will say it spent a ton, had the smartest advisors, and did everything reasonable. In short, Kroger tried hard and was thwarted by the regulators. Albertsons’ reply will clearly be that trying hard was not what Kroger promised. The contract the company signed was to get the deal done, come hell or high water, and because of its failure, Kroger should be forced to pay for its weak efforts and a failed merger.

description:

text:
The Nasdaq-100 is often described as a tech index, and most of the time that is fair. This week, tech stocks have been decimated, so maybe it's time to stop viewing it as a tech index. Tucked between the chipmakers and software giants are a handful of companies that sell soda, candy bars, and energy drinks, and a few of them are having a better year than the headlines suggest.

Monster Beverage(NASDAQ: MNST), Keurig Dr Pepper(NASDAQ: KDP), and Mondelez International(NASDAQ: MDLZ) each have something specific happening between now and the end of the year that makes October a reasonable time to look and consider buying.

Monster Beverage is bigger overseas than most people think

The easy read on Monster is that it sells caffeine to Americans. The more interesting read is in the numbers themselves: Sales to customers outside the U.S. rose 34.6% last quarter and now account for about 46% of the total, up from 41% a year earlier. That shift tells us why this ticker might be hot right now. Energy drinks are still an early habit in much of the world, and Monster is riding that with the Coca-Cola bottling system behind it.

According to online news site Food Navigator, Monster is accelerating global energy drink growth by leveraging Coca-Cola's distribution network, expanding into markets such as China, India, Southeast Asia, and Pakistan and introducing affordable, localized, sugar-free, and female-focused products to attract new consumers and increase market share.

Why October? The stock did a 2-for-1 split in August, which changes nothing about the business, but stock splits tend to draw a fresh look from smaller investors, and the company reports third-quarter results in early November. Buying before a report is a bet that the trend will hold, and it has held for a while. The risk worth naming is aluminum, which the company flagged as a cost pressure, along with the chance that regulators somewhere will decide to limit who can buy an energy drink.

Keurig Dr Pepper is about to become two companies

Keurig Dr Pepper closed its purchase of JDE Peet's in April and plans to split into two businesses in early 2027: a North American soda and water company anchored by Dr Pepper and a global coffee company with Peet's, L'OR, and Jacobs. The refreshment side grew sales 10% last quarter, with volume up 6.5%, which is strong for a soda business in any year.

The case for buying now is that the market tends to misprice conglomerates right before they break apart, and KDP reports on Nov. 3, its last full quarterly look before the separation work moves to the front burner. Anyone who buys in October gets shares of both companies when the split happens.

The risk is debt. The company expects to end 2026 at about 4.1 times leverage, and U.S. coffee sales fell 3.2% last quarter. The soda business is carrying the coffee business for now.

Mondelez is proving volume can grow again

Mondelez, the owner of Oreo and Cadbury, spent two years raising prices to cover a cocoa spike. The question was whether shoppers would keep buying once prices settled. Last quarter said yes: Volume and mix turned positive, emerging markets stayed strong, and the board raised the dividend 4%. The company also keeps doing small things that work, like the Toblerone and Biscoff tie-up announced in September.

Mondelez reports on Oct. 29, so this is the one pick where the catalyst lands inside the month. Management has said it is reinvesting behind its brands, which costs money in the short run, and that is the risk. If Europe does not keep improving, the market will not wait.

What investors should do with this information

None of these three is a secret, and each has a date circled on the calendar that could change how the market sees it. My practical move is simple: Pick the one whose risks you understand best, buy a starting position before the report instead of chasing it after, and plan to hold through whatever the quarter throws at you. Earnings season rewards patience far more than timing, and a good consumer brand bought in October is usually still a good one in April.

All three have taken a beating lately as investors sell off over high costs and jitters about tech. I think that's exactly the opportunity. These are durable businesses; they'll rebound, and the people who sit tight through the noise are the ones who get paid for it.

name: Nvidia
title: Ericsson CEO champions his silicon over Nvidia chips in RAN - Light Reading
description:
Might Ericsson also be persuaded of a GPU's attractions over conventional custom silicon?
For years, Ericsson has designed its own application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) for Layer 1, the slice of RAN software that covers the most demanding tasks.
Nokia and Nvidia insist GPUs offer advantages over custom silicon, allowing them to swap out normal RAN algorithms for more efficient AI.
The figures published by Ericsson, based on the continued use of custom silicon, are much lower.
It's the economy, stupid But economic factors play a critical role in the RAN choice between custom silicon and general-purpose chips, whether CPUs or GPUs.
text:
Ever since Nokia struck its $1 billion pact with Nvidia around this time last year, industry watchers have wondered if rival Ericsson might do something similar. With Nvidia's investment in Nokia came the revelation of plans by the Finnish vendor to design radio access network (RAN) products based on the huge chipmaker's graphics processing units (GPUs), ordinarily aimed at the data center. Might Ericsson also be persuaded of a GPU's attractions over conventional custom silicon?

The answer has been a polite but firm no, although not without a caveat. For years, Ericsson has designed its own application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) for Layer 1, the slice of RAN software that covers the most demanding tasks. In the 5G era, the strategy seemed to differentiate it from Nokia, which switched to a partnership with Marvell Technology for custom silicon after initial 5G setbacks with Intel. Under Nokia's latest plans, Nvidia will eventually replace Marvell. Per Narvinger, Ericsson's new boss, sees no reason to follow by substituting GPUs for Ericsson's ASICs.

"We have disaggregated our software and hardware, meaning we have a lot of flexibility on what path to embark on in the future," he told equity analysts on Ericsson's call about third-quarter results last week. "Having said that, right now, we see that it's an extraordinary asset to have your own ASICs. That really makes it possible for us to get our functionality fast. It makes it possible for us to be very cost competitive."

The remarks came after Narvinger was asked if Ericsson had closed the door on putting GPUs into the baseband responsible for RAN compute. Nokia and Nvidia insist GPUs offer advantages over custom silicon, allowing them to swap out normal RAN algorithms for more efficient AI. If evidence of that is provided by ongoing trials with prominent operators like T-Mobile US, Ericsson's defense of custom silicon could start to look seriously misguided.

The spectre of efficiency

But Ericsson's experts clearly doubt Nokia can realize any significant advantages with a GPU RAN. Algorithms and models deployed in a RAN are constrained by factors such as the transmission time interval, which means important calculations cannot take longer than 500 microseconds. Software designed to work in these conditions does not require the processing muscle of a GPU – or so the argument goes.

Nokia claims it can double the spectral efficiency of a network by 2028 with its GPU strategy. The figures published by Ericsson, based on the continued use of custom silicon, are much lower. But various experts including Marcus Weldon, a former Nokia chief technology officer, reckon the huge improvements Nokia has talked about will be limited to a small number of use cases.

The baseline for comparison has also not been specified, but significant gains would naturally be easier to achieve on a badly performing network. "A site already achieving near-theoretical efficiency under classical processing has less headroom for AI-driven improvement than a site operating well below its theoretical ceiling due to interference, channel estimation errors, or suboptimal scheduling," said Chetan Sharma, the founder of Chetan Sharma Consulting, in a recently published white paper.

Importantly, too, Nokia's approach requires operators to install GPUs in their networks, while Ericsson boasts commercially deployed silicon that can already support new AI features such as AI-native link adaptation, a RAN algorithm. "It's been around in the industry for as long as I've been, so more than three decades, and now replacing that with an AI model we get 10% gain in spectral efficiency," said Narvinger. "Today, we have that deployed commercially with three operators, and we have more than 60,000 basestations running this functionality."

Even so, Narvinger told analysts that Ericsson is "not ruling out any other platform," and the Swedish company has partly hedged its bets. The "disaggregation" cited by Narvinger refers to Ericsson's separate virtual or cloud RAN development track, which today runs most Layer 1 functions on Intel's general-purpose central processing units (CPUs). Only a single resource-hungry task – forward error correction (FEC) – is offloaded to a hardware accelerator, which Intel supplies and combines with its latest CPUs.

Ericsson is now confident it could move the software for the CPU-hosted functions to other CPU platforms after small tweaks. Such platforms might include AMD, which uses the same x86 architecture as Intel, or even a processor based on Arm, a rival architecture. During trials, it already claims to have ported software to an Arm-based CPU offered by Nvidia. A GPU, in this kind of scenario, could function as the FEC hardware accelerator while supporting other AI needs.

It's the economy, stupid

But economic factors play a critical role in the RAN choice between custom silicon and general-purpose chips, whether CPUs or GPUs. Ericsson's naysayers insist it will not be able to sustain custom silicon investment in what Narvinger himself describes as a "flat" RAN market. General-purpose processors, by contrast, have a much bigger target market and better returns.

It's an argument Narvinger has previously rejected on the grounds that Ericsson is not starting from scratch and facing substantial upfront costs, but instead building on years of activity. He and other senior executives at Ericsson also think CPUs and GPUs will prove costlier because of their need – as general-purpose chips – to support features that might never be used. Ericsson's latest earnings report, notably, came with yet another warning about rising component costs driven by the AI boom.

At the RAN-making mobile networks business group responsible for almost two thirds of Ericsson's revenues, the gross margin shrank by 0.2 percentage points year-over-year for the quarter, to 49.8%, as sales rose 9%, to 38.7 billion Swedish kronor (US$3.9 billion). But the unit's operating margin improved by 1.8 percentage points, to 21.8%, and it has been far more profitable than Nokia's equivalent business unit.

Yet to report third-quarter results, Nokia reported a second-quarter operating margin of 11.6% at its mobile infrastructure group, which includes core software and licensing activities besides the RAN business. That was down from 12.2% the year before. If Narvinger is right, a RAN strategy based on the use of GPUs may squeeze those margins in future quarters.

Nokia's deal with Nvidia might have been the fruit of economic necessity rather than about architectural roadmaps. Existing commercial partner Marvell is known to have had concerns about the returns it could generate from developing custom silicon products for Nokia after the Finnish company lost valuable US market share in a shrinking RAN sector. A deal with Intel seemed unlikely after Nokia's RAN relationship with the chipmaker was damaged by those initial 5G setbacks. In the absence of other viable suppliers, Nvidia might have been the only option Nokia had.

text:
The ECB has authorised the Italian banking group to cross the 30% ownership threshold and increase its holding further without an upper limit.

UniCredit described the decision as an important milestone in its proposed acquisition and said it reflected the ECB’s confidence in the group’s financial strength and standing within the European banking sector.

Control Could Follow by Year-End

The remaining regulatory approvals and transaction conditions are expected to be completed around the end of the year.

At that point, UniCredit expects to hold approximately 50% of Commerzbank’s voting rights, giving it effective control of the bank.

The development marks a significant turn in a takeover battle that Commerzbank had initially resisted. The German lender eventually entered talks with UniCredit in July after months of opposition to the Italian bank’s growing stake.

Commerzbank Restructuring Adds to the Strategic Backdrop

The potential change of control comes as Commerzbank continues a substantial restructuring programme.

The bank announced 3,900 job cuts in 2025 and a further 3,000 reductions in May, while simultaneously increasing investment in artificial intelligence and other technology-led efficiency measures.

For the wider European banking sector, the deal would represent another important test of cross-border consolidation.

European policymakers have long argued that the region’s banking market remains too fragmented, limiting scale and efficiency compared with larger US institutions.

UniCredit’s progress therefore carries significance beyond the two banks involved.

If the remaining approvals are secured, the transaction would create a more powerful cross-border banking group and provide one of the clearest recent examples of consolidation beginning to reshape Europe’s financial landscape.

text:
METiS TechBio (7666.HK) announced a strategic collaboration with Eli Lilly (LLY) and Company focused on developing next-generation lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery of medicines to specify tissues in the body.

Lipid nanoparticles are tiny carriers used to transport therapeutic molecules into cells. Improving their ability to target specific tissues could help enhance the effectiveness of a wide range of treatments while potentially reducing unwanted effects.

Under the agreement, METiS will use its proprietary AI-driven AiLNP platform to discover and optimize new ionizable lipids and LNP delivery systems. Lilly will contribute its drug discovery, development and commercialization expertise to help advance the research program.

The collaboration aims to develop tissue-specific delivery technologies that could improve how therapies are distributed within the body, potentially expanding the use of LNP-based medicines across multiple disease areas.

Under the terms of the deal, METiS is eligible to receive an upfront payment in the low double-digit millions of dollars, along with up to approximately $1.1 billion in development, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments. The company is also eligible to receive tiered royalties in the single-digit percentage range on future product sales resulting from the collaboration.

The agreement combines METiS'artificial intelligence-based approach to designing and optimizing drug-delivery system with Lilly's experience in bringing new medicines through clinical development and commercialization.

The collaboration represents the latest effort by pharmaceutical companies to use artificial intelligence and advanced delivery technologies to improve the precision and effectiveness to next-generation therapies.

text:
It’s quite rare, but in the 5,800 hotels located in more than 110 countries that the Accor group operates, a leading tourist destination was missing today: the Dominican Republic. In a market where American and Spanish groups are widely represented, this absence will now be only temporary, since the French group has just announced a series of developments across the country. This applies both in the capital Saint-Domingue and in the popular leisure areas for incentive stays such as Miches, the Bay of Samana or Punta Cana.

On the occasion of the Dominican Republic Week in France, the hotel group signed several agreements or protocol agreements for more than 20 hotels under construction. This represents a total of 6,000 rooms under preparation, equivalent to 6.5 % of the Dominican Republic’s hotel capacity.« We are not just investing in this market; we are actively participating in its structuring., commented Camil Yazbeck, General Manager of the Development of Premium, Mid-Range and Economy Brands at Accor. The Dominican Republic represents a market in which tourism growth, infrastructure-related investments, and international demand are advancing in concert and at a rapid pace. ".

From large conferences to incentive stays

Driven by the state-owned bank Banreservas, and supported by Dominican and international investors, this development plan targets both business travelers and tourists who come to relax under the Caribbean sun. A symbol of an expansion that is not only aimed at leisure clientele, a Pullman hotel will soon be established in Juan Dolio, just above a 4,000-seat convention center currently under construction. Located in the east of the capital, near the Las Américas International Airport, this 400-key hotel will help make it possible to organize international congresses and events on the Dominican coastline.

In addition to supporting Rep« Dom’’s expansion ambitions in the MICE segment, Accor is strengthening its offering of urban hotels with a Swissôtel expected in Saint-Domingue, combining 75 keys and 180 residences for long-term stays, while an ibis budget with 170 rooms will be located near the capital’s airport in 2028. In the meantime, a 100-key ibis hotel is also planned at Punta Cana airport. Meanwhile, business and leisure travelers will find two new Novotel in the seaside city, the Novotel Punta Cana starting in 2027, followed by the Novotel Punta Cana Downtown. An ibis Styles is also expected in Punta Cana in 2030, on the main road leading to the destination.

Through the recently concluded development agreements, the ibis brand family is also involved in the structuring of a network of budget hotels that meet international standards in the country’s major cities – Saint-Domingue, Santiago, Puerto Plata, Las Terrenas and Higüey – as well as in airport areas, as seen above.

Multibrand complexes

Of course, this development plan would not be complete without what makes the destination so appealing: the large resort complexes. In this context, Accor will install several of these brands in a 207-hectare complex currently being built along the coast in Miches. This will meet all the expectations of MICE groups with the large Grand Mercure and Novotel with 1,000 keys, and a Swissôtel with 250 rooms. If, in a more economical style, a luxurious Fairmont could also be added to complete the project.

Another tourist destination, more focused on nature and well-being, Cabo Engaño, at the easternmost tip of the country, is expected to see the emergence of an imposing 1,000-room Mövenpick hotel, complemented by a 150-key Swissôtel hotel and 100 «branded residences». A long-stay component will also be offered by a 150-room Tribe hotel accompanied by 350 Tribe Living residences.

Finally, the Handwritten Collection brand is also involved in this expansion with two projects: one in Cabrera, on the north side, with a 95-key boutique hotel expected in 2028, and the other, larger in Miches with a 350-room complex located on the edge of a lagoon facing the Bay of Samana. For an opening scheduled for 2030.

text:
Salesforce has signed a definitive agreement to acquire customer engagement platform Braze for approximately $5.66 billion in enterprise value, expanding Salesforce’s Marketing Cloud and broader Customer 360 platform with additional real-time customer engagement and AI decisioning capabilities.

Under the agreement, holders of Braze Class A common stock will receive $47.50 in cash for each share. The transaction is expected to close during Salesforce’s fiscal year 2028, subject to approval by Braze shareholders, required regulatory clearances, and other customary closing conditions.

Braze provides technology that enables marketers to respond to customer behavior in real time and coordinate personalized experiences across mobile applications, websites, email, SMS, WhatsApp, and other channels. Its cloud-native event-streaming architecture continuously updates customer profiles and adjusts customer journeys as new behavioral data arrives.

BrazeAI extends the platform with AI-powered capabilities that optimize content, offers, communication channels, and timing. Following the acquisition, Salesforce expects to combine these capabilities with its Data 360, Customer 360, Agentforce, and SIForce platforms.

Within Customer 360, Salesforce said Braze would strengthen Marketing Cloud’s cross-channel personalization capabilities and help brands use real-time customer data to deliver more relevant experiences at scale. The companies also plan to maintain an open and composable approach that lets customers continue working with a range of data platforms, tools, and technology partners.

Braze serves approximately 2,770 customers, including Canva, Dairy Queen, Equinox, Instacart, Urban Outfitters, and Venmo. The company is led by co-founders Bill Magnuson and Jon Hyman and brings expertise in mobile experiences, customer engagement, and data engineering.

Salesforce said the acquisition aligns with its strategy of expanding through both internal product development and acquisitions as businesses increasingly adopt agentic AI systems capable of interpreting customer information, making decisions, and acting in real time.

The company does not anticipate any change to its fiscal year 2027 guidance as a result of the transaction.

J.P. Morgan Securities is serving as exclusive financial advisor to Salesforce, with Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz and Covington & Burling serving as legal counsel. Qatalyst Partners is acting as exclusive financial advisor to Braze, while Davis Polk & Wardwell is serving as Braze’s legal counsel.

KEY QUOTES:

“Every interaction is an opportunity to wow your customers. Most of that wow comes from knowing your customer, and responding at just the right moment. Braze was built to turn live customer behavior into personalized engagement at scale. Bringing that capability together with Salesforce Marketing Cloud, CRM, and Data 360 will deliver that wow moment in every customer interaction.”

Patrick Stokes, President, Applications And Marketing At Salesforce

“Braze was built on the conviction that marketers and their creativity are a brand’s ultimate competitive advantage. This past year we shipped at the fastest pace in our history, and BrazeAI is helping marketers get their best ideas live faster. Salesforce shares our commitment to marketers, and we’ll continue building as Braze and investing in the Braze community of customers and partners who built this company with us. Salesforce’s platform will help us innovate faster and together we’ll help marketers around the world build deeper, more lasting relationships with their customers.”

text:
MILAN, Oct 20 (Reuters) - Italy's second-largest bank, UniCredit, said on Tuesday it was bringing its domestic securities services unit back in-house, two decades after outsourcing the business to Societe Generale.

The bank confirmed in a statement what Reuters had first reported late on Monday citing a union document.

"The transfer supports the ... bank's previously announced plan to internalise key back-office activities for securities services, establishing harmonised suppliers and processes across Italy and Germany and creating a more streamlined, resilient and scalable operating model," it said.

The unit, which looks after investors' securities and handles related administrative services, comprises 54 staff who will be transferred to UniCredit from Societe Generale Securities Services.

When Societe Generale acquired the business from UniCredit in 2006 the unit had a staff of 435.

The transaction marked Societe Generale's entry into the Italian market. The French bank said earlier this month it had built solid client relationships in Italy over the past two decades and considered it a strategic market for the group.

With nearly €6 trillion of assets under custody, Societe Generale is one of Europe's top three providers of securities services and ranks among the top 10 globally.

UniCredit said the move would support the creation of more than 200 roles, partly through the retraining of existing employees, as part of its securities services transformation programme.

(Reporting by Valentina Za; Editing by Cynthia Osterman, Louise Heavens and Keith Weir)

description:
At the Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin, the German government entered into an agreement with Nvidia on Monday, when Chancellor Friedrich Merz opened the two-day event by addressing Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO.
Nvidia provided further details in a company blog post, stating that Merz and two ministries have entered into a joint plan with it.

text:
At the Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin, the German government entered into an agreement with Nvidia on Monday, when Chancellor Friedrich Merz opened the two-day event by addressing Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO.

The economy ministry has entered into a memorandum of understanding with the chipmaker but has provided no further details; the agreement comes after reports last week that Germany would announce a partnership with Nvidia at the summit.

Nvidia provided further details in a company blog post, stating that Merz and two ministries have entered into a joint plan with it. The objective is to develop AI that can operate robots, machines, and cars; this is referred to as physical AI.

Nvidia has also identified four German startups that it intends to invest in, as part of its nearly $10bn commitment in Europe. These companies are Agile Robots, Avelios Medical, Mirelo and Reflex Aerospace. Moreover, Siemens and Nvidia have agreed to collaborate on AI-operated factories.

The deals are part of a nearly $10bn commitment to companies, universities and research institutions across Europe.

Agile Robots makes AI-powered robots, from robotic arms to its Agile ONE humanoid, for factories, logistics and healthcare. Avelios Medical builds a hospital information system with AI at its core that runs clinical and administrative work so doctors and nurses can spend more time with patients.

Mirelo develops AI models that create sound effects, speech and music to match video. Berlin-based Reflex Aerospace designs and builds satellites that it says can be ready for launch in about 12 months, rather than years.

“We are fully committed to be one of the most advanced places in the world, not just in the European Union, but in the world to work with AI, to integrate AI into our industry,” Merz said.

He also stated that artificial intelligence was driving major changes in Germany’s economy and that cooperation with Nvidia was important to its future. Merz is under pressure to boost growth as German car manufacturers, chemical companies and engineers face strong overseas competition.

“The biggest advantage we have in Germany is our so-called Mittelstand,” Merz said. “Please open your doors for AI to make use of your data. This is a real secret and a real advantage for Germany to make use of all the data which is already available in our companies.”

At the same time, a number of companies and investors, such as Siemens and Deutsche Bank, put out an estimate. As Reuters reports, this group expects up to 4.1 trillion euros (approximately 4.6 trillion dollars) in potential investment in Germany by 2035 in the areas of AI, energy and defence.

Siemens and Deutsche Bank established Made for Germany, a business initiative consisting of around 150 companies and investors. The initiative stated that its members intend to have invested more than €850bn by 2028, following an investment of over €200bn in 2025.

The German government’s website lists among the companies present at the summit Mercedes-Benz, Bayer, Lufthansa, Deutsche Telekom, BlackRock and Goldman Sachs. The summit will end on Tuesday, and Huang is expected to deliver a keynote speech at the Nvidia GTC Berlin conference on Wednesday.

“That knowledge belongs to you,” Huang said. “It cannot be replaced. AI can only augment your capability, it will not replace your capability. Take advantage of the technology. It’s a new instrument.”

name: Moody's
title: Moody's: Insurers Embrace AI but Struggle to Measure Returns - ProgramBusiness
description:
AI Adoption Across Insurance Operations Generative AI, including chatbots, copilots, and large language models, led adoption at 98%.
P&C insurers reported higher spending than life insurers.
Nearly 20% of P&C carriers allocated more than 10% of IT budgets to AI, compared with 7% of life insurers.
The agency also warned that advanced AI models could accelerate the exploitation of software vulnerabilities, increasing cybersecurity exposures.
Dependence on external AI models and cloud providers also increases insurers’ exposure to cybersecurity incidents involving critical technology vendors.
text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is now widely used among North American insurers and brokers, although many companies struggle to measure its financial benefits, according to a Moody’s Ratings survey.

The survey covered 58 companies across life, health, property and casualty (P&C), reinsurance, and brokerage sectors. About two-thirds reported broad AI deployment or multiple applications operating across core business functions. Meanwhile, 34% reported enterprise-wide deployment.

Moody’s said AI primarily improves operational efficiency rather than transforming insurers’ business models. The rating agency expects a neutral-to-positive credit impact, depending on implementation, data quality, and governance.

AI Adoption Across Insurance Operations

Generative AI, including chatbots, copilots, and large language models, led adoption at 98%. Traditional machine learning and predictive models followed at 79%, while 71% used agentic AI or workflow automation.

Among P&C insurers and reinsurers, 75% had deployed AI in operations. More than half used AI for underwriting and pricing, while half used it for claims, loss adjustment, and fraud detection. Only 19% reported production use in catastrophe and exposure management.

Life insurers primarily focused on customer service, distribution, underwriting, and operations.

Among brokers, 29% reported enterprise-wide deployment, 43% had multiple production applications, and 28% reported limited adoption.

AI Spending and Financial Returns

Respondents most frequently cited productivity improvements or avoided staffing increases (76%) and faster processing times (74%). P&C insurers also reported reduced loss severity, claims leakage, and loss adjustment expenses, along with improved combined ratios.

AI spending typically represented 2% to 10% of insurers’ IT budgets. However, 13% spent more than 10%.

P&C insurers reported higher spending than life insurers. Nearly 20% of P&C carriers allocated more than 10% of IT budgets to AI, compared with 7% of life insurers.

Despite widespread adoption, only 41% consistently quantified and tracked benefits for individual applications. Another 34% measured benefits without consistent tracking, while 24% primarily relied on qualitative assessments.

Moody’s attributed the measurement challenges in part to workflow redesign and temporary overlap between existing and new processes. Several insurers had not established formal timelines for evaluating returns.

The agency also noted that larger insurers generally have greater technology budgets and data resources than smaller competitors.

Implementation Challenges and Emerging Risks

Talent shortages topped the list of implementation challenges at 81%, followed by data quality at 71% and legacy-system integration at 62%.

Additionally, 47% cited regulatory uncertainty, while 88% said their AI governance principles aligned with regulatory guidance.

Moody’s identified increased operational, regulatory, litigation, and third-party vendor risks associated with AI adoption.

The agency also warned that advanced AI models could accelerate the exploitation of software vulnerabilities, increasing cybersecurity exposures.

As an example, Moody’s cited Anthropic’s Mythos model, which identified serious vulnerabilities in major operating systems and browsers in April 2026.

Dependence on external AI models and cloud providers also increases insurers’ exposure to cybersecurity incidents involving critical technology vendors.

name: Microsoft
title: Microsoft's New AI Chip Could Change the Economics of AI - The Globe and Mail
description:
Its new Maia 300 chip is a clear sign and a potential catalyst ahead of earnings.
It expects Maia 300 to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems.
Beyond Maia: Physical AI Is a Future Catalyst Physical AI, especially humanoid robots, is a later catalyst.
What Investors Should Watch in Microsoft's Upcoming Earnings Analysts expect earnings per share (EPS) of about $4.72 on revenue of $90.6 billion.
While Maia 300 won't begin deployment until 2027, it could eventually help Microsoft manage the costs of its expanding AI infrastructure.
text:
Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ: MSFT) wants to stop renting its AI future from NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ: NVDA). Its new Maia 300 chip is a clear sign and a potential catalyst ahead of earnings.

Microsoft plans to deploy Maia chips at a multi-gigawatt scale starting in 2027. It expects Maia 300 to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems.

More importantly, Microsoft says Maia will become the primary inference hardware for Microsoft’s own products. That speaks to the question hanging over every AI stock: Is this a bubble?

The bear case is simple. Generative AI is becoming a commodity. Chatbots are interchangeable, and token prices keep falling. Agentic AI may follow the same path. If the product is a commodity, why spend hundreds of billions on data centers?

Falling token prices don't necessarily mean weaker demand. Cheaper tokens can encourage more AI use, especially as agents take on increasingly complex tasks. Commodity markets don’t punish everyone equally, though. They reward the low-cost producer. Maia 300 is Microsoft’s attempt to become that producer.

Investors will get a fresh read on the strategy soon. Microsoft is estimated to report first-quarter fiscal year 2027 (FY2027) results after the close on Wednesday, Oct. 28.

Maia 300 Targets the Real Constraint: Power

Electricity availability is becoming a major constraint on data center growth, even as demand increases. That makes tokens per megawatt an important measure of efficiency.

Maia 300's compute chiplets are built on Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company’s (NYSE: TSM) N2P process, and the chip includes eight stacks of HBM4 memory. A full rack holds 96 chips. Microsoft says that a full rack delivers up to seven times the token throughput of a Maia 200 rack.

The chip targets long-context reasoning and multi-step agentic tasks. In other words, it was built for the workloads driving demand today.

Greater efficiency could allow Microsoft to process more AI workloads without a proportional increase in power consumption, potentially improving margins as usage grows.

The scale is meaningful, too. Reuters, citing The Information, reported that Microsoft ultimately aimed to secure manufacturing capacity for more than one million Maia 300 chips, although the company has not confirmed production targets. Microsoft plans to discuss its broader AI strategy at its Ignite conference in November.

Beyond Maia: Physical AI Is a Future Catalyst

Physical AI, especially humanoid robots, is a later catalyst. Counterpoint expects global humanoid shipments to top 50,000 units in 2026. That’s small next to agentic demand. But as adoption grows, robotics could create another source of demand for cloud-based AI services.

Microsoft won’t build robots. Instead, it’s positioning itself as the platform that trains, hosts and manages them. In January, Microsoft Research unveiled Rho-alpha, a robotics model that translates natural-language commands into robotic movements and incorporates tactile sensing. Microsoft plans to offer it through its Foundry platform.

The company also partnered with Hexagon Robotics in January to develop industrial humanoid applications, targeting automotive, aerospace, manufacturing, and logistics customers. Azure supports the cloud infrastructure behind that effort.

Here’s the link to Maia. Robot training and simulation already use cloud computing, while some inference happens on the robot itself. However, Microsoft is also exploring ways to shift inference workloads to edge and cloud infrastructure. If that approach gains traction, Maia's efficiency improvements could eventually help Microsoft serve those workloads at a lower cost.

Microsoft has not announced plans to use Maia for robotics, so the connection remains a possibility rather than an established use case. None of this will show up in the upcoming results. It’s optionality. But it gives Microsoft a potential second demand curve after AI agents.

Microsoft Stock Nears Highs as Analysts See More Upside

text:
Walmart on Tuesday announced a new joint membership combining its namesake chain and its subsidiary Sam’s Club, as the retailer leans further into convenience and value to win over cash-strapped shoppers.

The membership, which combines Walmart+ and Sam’s Club Plus, will cost $120 per year, according to the company. That price is nearly $100 less than buying individual annual memberships to each retailer, though there is no monthly payment option for the new deal. Both stores will continue to offer standalone options.

“We’re giving people a reason to expect more from their memberships,” Walmart CEO John Furner said in a statement. “For $120 a year, we’re raising expectations for what a membership can deliver: more money in their pockets and more time to call their own.”

The membership gives customers access to Sam’s Club warehouses, free delivery from both chains, a subscription to Peacock or Paramount+ streaming services, gas savings and 2% Sam’s Club cash on eligible purchases. Customers who already have accounts at both stores can link their accounts to receive the discount.

While Walmart’s customers often shop for routine, everyday essentials, Sam’s Club warehouses offer more opportunity to stock up on bulk purchases. A joint membership could allow the store models to complement one another, according to the company.

The announcement comes as Walmart bets on convenience to drive sales, especially as consumer wallets are squeezed by high gas and food prices.

In August, as Walmart reported fiscal second-quarter earnings, the company raised its outlook for the year, with Chief Financial Officer John David Rainey telling CNBC that consumer spending remained strong despite higher fuel prices. Even so, its stock fell at the time as its sales outlook disappointed Wall Street.

Rainey said in August that the company was lowering prices across various categories, including beef, adding that it’s well positioned to weather economic uncertainty because of its emphasis on value and its scale.

Meanwhile, Sam’s Club saw a 26% increase in e-commerce sales in the fiscal second quarter, driven by increased transactions and membership growth. The retailer, which also operates its own gas stations, reported net sales of $25.7 billion, including fuel, during that period.

The membership business — which is part of Walmart’s push to grow sales with higher profit margins — is already strong. Walmart reported a 17% increase globally in revenue from its membership in the fiscal second quarter with Walmart+ net adds notching a record second-quarter high. For Sam’s Club, that revenue number grew 6%.

Walmart added Tuesday that employees at both stores will also receive joint memberships as part of their benefits.

The company said any costs related to the changes in the membership program are not expected to materially impact the company’s fiscal third-quarter or full-year guidance.

text:
Philly’s life sciences community is seeing wins this fall, including a major deal for a local startup.

Digital pathology company Proscia agreed to be acquired by Agilent Technologies for $240 million.

Plus, the Small Business Administration selected the Science Center for a $1 million grant to connect biomanufacturing resources in the region.

Other sectors within Philly’s tech community are also seeing financial support. The Pew Center for Arts and Heritage donated $90,000 to a gaming exhibit at Drexel University this fall.

Scroll down for all the details and more Money Moves.

Agilent to acquire Proscia in $240M deal

Local digital pathology company Proscia last week announced that it entered a definitive agreement to be acquired by global lab technology company Agilent Technologies.

The deal is worth $240 million in cash, with the potential for an additional $30 million if certain milestones are met.

Until the deal closes in fiscal year 2027, it’s too early to say exactly how Proscia’s approximately 100-person team will mesh with Agilent, according to David West, cofounder and CEO of Proscia. However, the acquisition is just as much about merging products and market presence as it is about talent.

“We’ve got a great nucleus of talent here,” West told Technical.ly. “We’ve also got people all over the world. We’re going to continue looking for great talent in Philly, and creating a culture that is great for our people here.”

Proscia and Agilent had an existing relationship, including a 2022 distribution agreement that combined their products to create a new diagnostic pathology system, West said. Agilent develops lab instruments for diagnostics, while Proscia provides software to support those tools.

“We’re going from this partnership model to [being] a part of the same company,” West said. “That gives us more scale, allows us to execute faster and also brings different capabilities that we don’t have.”

The timing of the move made sense because of both the state of the industry and Proscia’s scale, West said. The company had hit revenue goals that made it attractive to companies like Agilent.

Over the last decade, scientists and healthcare workers have become more open to digital pathology. Advances in AI and drug development make Proscia’s tech more enticing, he added.

West founded Proscia in 2014 as a biomedical engineering student at Johns Hopkins University. The company moved from Baltimore to Philly in 2018 to access more talent, West previously said.

Science Center gets $1M to launch biomanufacturing cluster

The Science Center received $1 million from the US Small Business Administration (SBA) to establish the Mid-Atlantic Biomanufacturing Scale-Up Cluster.

The money will support the Science Center’s programming related to the industry, which uses microorganisms or cells to grow or make products. The effort will connect related resources in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, Maryland and DC.

“We’re really looking to navigate the biomanufacturing ecosystem on behalf of businesses to help them more readily access what is already there,” Heath Naquin, senior vice president of innovation and new ventures at the Science Center, told Technical.ly.

The initiative will be similar to its Capital Readiness Program, which prepares startup founders for fundraising. Funding from the SBA will support the Science Center’s efforts to educate early-stage companies about what they need to do to get ready for manufacturing and connect them with experts in the space.

The cluster will also help midsize companies make connections in the domestic manufacturing sector, according to Naquin.

Programs will be open to companies from across the country. The Science Center is focused on drawing attention to resources in the Greater Philadelphia region and creating lasting economic development opportunities, Naquin said.

“If we’re able to help, in some way, bring a company from wherever to establish their biomanufacturing facilities here,” Naquin said, “that goes to create jobs, that goes to create other things, that’s a win.”

This funding comes from the SBA’s Regional Innovation Clusters program, which selected nine orgs across the country this cycle to receive grants totaling more than $7 million. The sectors range widely from defense to transportation, aiming to connect entrepreneurs with applicable resources.

Drexel opens interactive gaming exhibit with $90k grant

A new video game-focused exhibit opened at Drexel University last week thanks to a $90,000 grant from the Pew Center for Arts and Heritage.

The interactive exhibit features games and displays from artists, historians and designers that explore the culture and community around gaming, co-organizer Christopher Grant told Technical.ly.

“Having a space to enjoy and share in what is often a very isolated hobby or isolated interest,” Grant said, “being able to share that in person with people is just very unusual.”

Some of the exhibit’s displays include a timeline of queer gaming history put together by local Temple University and Drexel professors and a virtual reality experience based on Taiwan’s period of martial law.

The group aims to challenge people’s existing ideas about gaming.

“Especially for folks who maybe don’t think of it as something that would fit into a traditional art gallery,” Grant said, “that they might be pressured to reexamine that bias and why they think of it.”

title: Albertsons begins its $8B trial against Kroger over failed merger - Idaho Business Review
description:
The bench trial is scheduled to run two weeks in Delaware’s Court of Chancery in front of Vice Chancellor Lori Will.
In December 2024, federal and state courts blocked the deal and Albertsons immediately terminated the merger, which Ohio-based Kroger said cut off its ability to appeal.
Kroger said in its court papers Albertsons was misreading the merger agreement and said that it kept its obligations, pinning the deal failure on regulatory opposition.
Kroger said it will prove at the trial that Albertsons isn’t entitled to the termination fee because it claims Albertsons undermined Kroger’s ability to negotiate.
Dozens of other potential witnesses include deal advisers, expert witnesses and current and former executives and directors.
text:
WILMINGTON, DEL.―Grocery chain Albertsons Companies will begin making its case in court on Monday for more than $8 billion in damages against larger rival Kroger for allegedly sinking their agreed $24.6 billion merger two years ago.

Boise-based Albertsons, whose chains include Safeway, Acme and Kings Food Markets, claims that Kroger broke its commitment to obtain regulatory approval for the deal by refusing to sell a sufficient number of stores. As a result, Albertsons said it is owed a premium of up to $6.88 billion the deal would have delivered to its shareholders, as well as the $600 million termination fee and more than $1 billion in tax adjustments.

The bench trial is scheduled to run two weeks in Delaware’s Court of Chancery in front of Vice Chancellor Lori Will. Rulings often take months after the trial ends and the outcome can be appealed to the Delaware Supreme Court.

The 2022 merger was meant to position the two companies and their 5,000 stores to better compete with newer entrants into grocery markets such as Walmart, Costco, Amazon and Aldi.

However, combining the largest and second-largest U.S. grocers was challenged by states and the administration of Democratic President Joe Biden, which argued the deal would remove direct competition and lead to higher prices at checkout.

In December 2024, federal and state courts blocked the deal and Albertsons immediately terminated the merger, which Ohio-based Kroger said cut off its ability to appeal.

Since the termination, Kroger’s stock has risen about 4% and Albertsons has lost nearly 30%, both lagging the S&P 500 index, which rose by more than a quarter.

The trial comes a week after Albertsons unveiled a cost-cutting review of its business and after Kroger, which owns the Dillons, Ralphs and Fred Meyer chains, planned to cut 3,000 jobs and invest in technology to lower prices.

Albertsons said that Kroger violated what it claimed was an obligation to take “any and all actions” to get antitrust approval, up to selling 650 stores.

Albertsons described in court papers the various divestiture packages that Kroger offered regulators as an attempt to minimize what it had to sell to protect the profitability of the post-merger business, rather than to get regulatory clearance.

It said Kroger created a $400 million executive bonus pool to encourage senior managers to take a highly aggressive approach to demands from regulators.

Kroger said in its court papers Albertsons was misreading the merger agreement and said that it kept its obligations, pinning the deal failure on regulatory opposition. It said that the Biden administration wanted it to sell more than 650 stores and courts blocked the merger because they took a narrow view of the grocery market by excluding Amazon, Costco and others.

Albertsons CEO could be witness

Kroger spent more than $1 billion and tens of thousands of hours of employee and adviser time trying to close the deal, which it said was evidence it was not willfully breaching the merger agreement.

Kroger said it will prove at the trial that Albertsons isn’t entitled to the termination fee because it claims Albertsons undermined Kroger’s ability to negotiate. It blamed that in part on allegedly unauthorized communications about the divestment plan by Susan Morris, who is now Albertsons’ CEO. Albertsons said there is zero evidence Morris shared sensitive information.

In addition to Morris, other potential witnesses include Rodney McMullen and Vivek Sankaran, who were CEOs of Kroger and Albertsons respectively at the time of the merger but who have since been replaced, according to court documents.

Dozens of other potential witnesses include deal advisers, expert witnesses and current and former executives and directors.

Reporting by Tom Hals in Wilmington, Delaware; Editing by Cynthia Osterman.

title: Walmart's Flipkart is quietly building a food delivery challenger in India | TechCrunch
description:
Flipkart, the Walmart-owned Indian e-commerce giant, is preparing to challenge India’s food-delivery duopoly of Zomato and Swiggy.
Flipkart is not the only company trying to shake up India’s food-delivery market.
Flipkart is not the first deep-pocketed company to try breaking into India’s food-delivery market.
Daryani sees one important difference between Flipkart and the companies that tried food delivery before it.
Flipkart is doing the reverse, using its established e-commerce business and growing quick-commerce operations as a springboard into food delivery.
text:
Flipkart, the Walmart-owned Indian e-commerce giant, is preparing to challenge India’s food-delivery duopoly of Zomato and Swiggy. It is entering a fiercely competitive market that has defeated even previous attempts by Amazon and Google to break in.

The Bengaluru-based company is testing its food-delivery service internally and has expanded the trial from a few hundred employees to upwards of 8,000, according to two people familiar with the matter. It has also deployed a dedicated fleet of riders through its logistics arm, Ekart, separate from the riders who handle its quick-commerce deliveries, as it prepares for a public launch.

The employee-only service appears as a separate tab on Flipkart’s main shopping app, alongside its Minutes quick-commerce offering and travel bookings, TechCrunch has learned. It draws on restaurants listed through ONDC, a government-backed network that connects online buyers and sellers across different platforms, as well as restaurants that Flipkart signed up directly.

Riders wearing jerseys bearing the “Eat-in by Minutes” branding have also begun fulfilling orders on the streets of Bengaluru, the southern Indian city where Flipkart is headquartered.

As Flipkart expands its food-delivery operations, it is entering a market that the brokerage firm Bernstein estimates is growing 18% to 20% a year. Online delivery, though, still accounts for just over 15% of India’s broader food-services industry. Zomato, owned by Eternal, and Swiggy together serve an estimated 85 million to 95 million paying customers a year, per Bernstein. That figure shows how dominant the two are, and how much room newcomers have to grow online food ordering in the world’s most populous country, which has more than a billion internet subscriptions.

Flipkart is not the only company trying to shake up India’s food-delivery market. Ride-hailing company Rapido, which has already given Uber and its Indian rival Ola a tough fight, has been expanding Ownly, its food-delivery service that charges restaurants zero commission. Meanwhile, Swiggy has launched Toing, a separate app aimed at customers looking for cheaper meals. Both moves reflect growing pressure on the industry’s existing pricing model and the commissions that restaurants pay.

“Monopoly is bad, but duopoly is more pathetic,” said Sagar Daryani, president of the New Delhi-headquartered National Restaurant Association of India, which represents over 500,000 restaurants nationwide. “What one does, the other follows suit.”

Daryani argued that restaurants have long needed alternatives to the two dominant platforms.

Flipkart is not the first deep-pocketed company to try breaking into India’s food-delivery market. In 2020, Amazon launched a food-ordering service in Bengaluru, but it shut the service down two years later. Google’s Areo app, which offered food ordering alongside other services, also failed to gain traction. Uber also left the market in 2020, selling its Uber Eats business in India to Zomato.

Daryani sees one important difference between Flipkart and the companies that tried food delivery before it. Zomato and Swiggy built their businesses around delivering meals before expanding into quick commerce. Flipkart is doing the reverse, using its established e-commerce business and growing quick-commerce operations as a springboard into food delivery.

“Flipkart’s quick commerce benefit will get passed on to food delivery, so it will be leaner, more efficient,” Daryani told TechCrunch.

Restaurants are also hoping that new entrants will bring down the cost of selling meals online. Daryani, also co-founder and CEO of the dumpling chain Wow! Momo Foods, said Flipkart has proposed a base commission of about 10%, compared with the 20% to 25% that restaurants typically pay Zomato and Swiggy.

Commissions are only part of the expense, though. Once advertising, discounts, and other promotional costs are factored in, restaurants can end up spending 40% to 50% of an order’s value on the established platforms, Daryani told TechCrunch. He expects Flipkart to keep that total cost closer to 15% to 16%, which could mean restaurants keep more money from each order.

Nonetheless, getting restaurants on board is one thing and winning over customers is another. Bernstein estimates that new entrants could save customers just ₹20 to ₹30 (around 20–30 cents) per order by operating more efficiently, which may not be enough to draw customers away from Zomato and Swiggy. The two incumbents could also offer deeper discounts to keep them.

Flipkart is not planning to stay in Bengaluru for long. The company has told restaurants that it expects to launch its food-delivery service publicly by the end of October and to expand to five or six cities by the end of this year, Daryani told TechCrunch.

The food-delivery push also comes as Flipkart’s long-awaited stock-market listing remains uncertain. Chief Executive Kalyan Krishnamurthy (pictured above) recently declined to give a timetable for an IPO, even as the company continues to expand into businesses that could bring customers back to its app more frequently.

Flipkart’s expansion comes as competition in India’s e-commerce market intensifies. Quick-commerce platforms that started by delivering groceries in minutes now sell even the latest iPhones and other discretionary purchases, putting them in more direct competition with Flipkart and Amazon.

Flipkart did not respond to a request for comments.
