Alphabet (GOOG -0.62%) (GOOGL -0.75%), which has been building its own custom AI chips for longer than any of its competitors, has seen strong adoption of its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) by its Google Cloud customers for training and inference. Apple used TPUs to train Apple Intelligence, and Anthropic is using gigawatts worth of TPUs to develop its large language models.

While Nvidia can continue to grow sales extremely quickly, other chipmakers' growth rates are likely to outpace it. That's reflected in its P/E valuation, which now sits below those of its biggest rivals.

Microsoft could be Marvell's fastest-growing customer

During its 2026 investor day this month, Marvell said it expects that it will grow its share of the custom AI accelerator market over the next five years. Its work on the Maia 300 is likely a big reason why. Microsoft's plan to make that processor the primary inference system for its products and services is in line with earlier reports that it will make a big step up in custom silicon orders starting next year.

The revenue opportunity for Marvell is huge. Microsoft will spend approximately $175 billion in capital expenditures on data centers over the next year. text:
Preparations for the 2027 budget are also taking centre stage in Bangkok. And personal income tax remains one of the key issues under discussion, even after the figures from the DPB were released. Returning to the subject is the Minister for the Economy Giancarlo Giorgetti, who was questioned on the sidelines of the meetings IMF meetings: ‘As regards personal income tax (IRPEF), given that all the pieces of the puzzle are currently coming together to make way for measures, the key decision we face is whether to implement selective or across-the-board measures.’

Collegial decision

The decision will be a collective one. As Giorgetti explained, ‘it is not right for the minister to decide alone; we will assess the situation together with the parties, the leadership and President Meloni. Two weeks ago I had an overview of income and expenditure; I’m not exactly optimistic, but we are heading in the right direction’.

Loading...

On the budget bill to wind up the parliamentary session next week

The timetable is tight. “Work on the Budget Bill will probably be finalised next week” and “we will present it to Parliament; as you know, a very constructive dialogue is continuing – I met Dombrovskis here too – regarding the NEC clauses on defence and energy”.

Banks’ contribution, but ‘sustainable’

Another key issue is how the banks are to contribute to the budget in terms of new revenue for the Treasury. The message from the head of Via XX Settembre is clear: “I can confirm that a contribution will be sought from the financial sector because we believe it can afford it, and we also believe that it will be a sustainable arrangement”. Giorgetti added that “keeping the spread under control is in everyone’s interest”, referring to the fact that the banks hold billions of euros’ worth of BTPs on their balance sheets.

On the prospect of possible legal challenges from the banks, the minister commented, ‘Every Italian could take the State to court for raising taxes. We will try to strike the right balance; I don’t think anyone will die as a result.’

name: Walmart
title: Amazon and Walmart Are Turning Retail Efficiency Into Someone Else's Expense
description:
Both developments illustrate a fundamental change in retail economics.
On Thursday (Oct. 15), Amazon introduced two new devices from Bee, the personal AI company it acquired last year.
Through the $11.99 monthly Bee Pro subscription, consumers can opt to connect the devices to Amazon.com and Alexa+.
The Next Retail Advantage Is Who Controls the Handoff Walmart’s robotics and Amazon’s conversational AI appear to address opposite ends of the retail value chain.
The other seeks to improve the identification and conversion of consumer demand.
text:
As Walmart pushes robotics deeper into its distribution network, and Amazon brings artificial intelligence into consumers’ everyday conversations with new product launches across its Bee wearable line, the two retail giants are pursuing different versions of the same economic ambition: reducing the distance between consumer demand and a completed sale.

But the more consequential story isn’t what their technology eliminates. It’s what happens to the costs, risks and commercial opportunities left behind.

Warehouse automation can reduce labor-intensive handling while requiring suppliers to redesign packaging and shipping operations. AI assistants can eliminate the need to search for products while giving technology platforms greater influence over which brands consumers discover and ultimately buy.

Both developments illustrate a fundamental change in retail economics. Innovation is no longer simply reducing the cost of commerce. It is changing which businesses bear that cost, which ones capture the savings and who controls the transaction.

See also: Amazon and Walmart Want Merchants’ Software Budgets

Walmart’s Robots Are Changing the Economics Outside the Warehouse

Walmart’s warehouse modernization program has become one of retail’s most ambitious experiments in industrial automation. The company has been deploying robotics and automated systems across its distribution network, seeking improvements in inventory handling, fulfillment productivity and operating efficiency.

Recent reporting has also highlighted the engineering challenges involved in automating the movement of everyday consumer merchandise. A warehouse full of machines, after all, still has to process products designed for a world of human workers.

And when a retailer changes the physical requirements of its distribution infrastructure, suppliers may have to change how merchandise arrives. Packaging dimensions, labeling, case configurations and shipping specifications can become prerequisites for participating efficiently in the network. The result is a potentially uncomfortable contradiction: A retailer’s investment in operational efficiency can generate new expenses elsewhere in its supply chain.

If Walmart captures productivity gains while suppliers shoulder substantial implementation costs, the financial returns will look very different depending on whose balance sheet is being examined.

Read more: Amazon Builds Its Own Answer to Walmart’s 5,000 Stores

Amazon Wants to Capture Demand Before It Becomes a Search

If Walmart is changing the economics of getting products to consumers, Amazon is experimenting with changing the economics of discovering what consumers want in the first place.

On Thursday (Oct. 15), Amazon introduced two new devices from Bee, the personal AI company it acquired last year. The $74.99 Bee Frontier wearable and forthcoming $99.99 Bee Eclipse phone attachment are designed to turn conversations into summaries, reminders and actionable recommendations. Through the $11.99 monthly Bee Pro subscription, consumers can opt to connect the devices to Amazon.com and Alexa+. Something mentioned in conversation, such as needing household supplies, can subsequently appear as a personalized product recommendation. Amazon says audio is processed and deleted, with users controlling their information.

The PYMNTS Intelligence report “Will the 2026 Shopping Season Go Agentic?“ found that roughly 132 million people have made a retail purchase with AI assistance, while 22% now begin online retail research in an artificial intelligence tool.

For brands, the opportunity is potentially lower-friction conversion. The risk is that another platform increasingly determines which products enter the consumer’s consideration set.

The Next Retail Advantage Is Who Controls the Handoff

Walmart’s robotics and Amazon’s conversational AI appear to address opposite ends of the retail value chain. One seeks to improve the physical movement of merchandise. The other seeks to improve the identification and conversion of consumer demand.

But both can strengthen the position of the platform that controls the infrastructure.

Walmart’s modernization illustrates how operational standards can affect the economics of supplier participation. Amazon’s AI expansion illustrates how ownership of the consumer interface can influence access to demand.

Walmart is working to control the transition from supplier inventory to automated fulfillment. Amazon is expanding its ability to connect consumer conversations with product discovery and shopping.

These are different operations, but they share a commercial characteristic: Whoever establishes the rules at the handoff can influence the economics of everyone participating.

That influence does not guarantee profits. Walmart’s automation difficulties demonstrate that owning infrastructure can bring significant capital, maintenance and execution costs. Amazon’s Bee expansion faces unresolved questions about consumer adoption, privacy expectations and whether personalized recommendations meaningfully change purchasing behavior.

text:
Project Status

October 2026: Northwestern IT is modernizing the University's telephone services by transitioning from Cisco to Microsoft Teams Voice. This change will better reflect how individuals and teams use phones across campus and provide a more integrated communications experience by bringing calls, voicemail, meetings, and messaging together in Microsoft Teams. Northwestern IT is partnering with technology teams across the University to plan a collaborative rollout of these changes between January 2027 and June 2028.

Background

As part of this transition, Northwestern IT is replacing the University-wide Cisco telephony platform and devices with Microsoft Teams Voice. Microsoft Teams Voice provides equivalent calling services and introduces a modern communications platform designed to support how people work today. The new service will offer calling options on computers, mobile devices, and Teams-certified phones. While core calling capabilities will remain available, some features and workflows will function differently than they do today.

Benefits to the Northwestern Community

Microsoft Teams Voice will modernize Northwestern's telephone service by integrating University calling into Microsoft Teams. This transition will maintain essential calling capabilities while delivering a more unified communications experience for calls, voicemail, meetings, and messaging. It will also simplify the telephony environment by reducing dependence on aging Cisco infrastructure and underutilized desk phones.

Connected experience: Manage calls, voicemail, meetings, and messaging in Microsoft Teams.

Flexible calling: Use a University number from a computer, mobile device, or approved Teams phone.

Modern service: Retire aging infrastructure and reduce the number of underused physical devices.

Goals and Objectives

The Teams Voice transition is designed to preserve essential telephone services while enabling schools, departments, and administrative units to adopt a modern, flexible communications platform that supports how people work today.

Preserve assigned University phone numbers and core calling capabilities.

Enable eligible users to make and receive calls through Teams desktop and mobile applications.

Migrate shared lines, call groups, and other existing services accurately.

Prepare affected users with guidance and support before and after migration.

Deliver a consistent calling experience across computers, mobile devices, and approved Teams-certified phones.

Provide Teams-certified phones where approved business requirements exist.

Minimize disruption to University operations throughout the transition.

Reduce complexity and ongoing costs by retiring aging telephony infrastructure and removing unused or underutilized desk phones.

Approach

The project will be implemented over 18 months in coordinated phases by school, unit, or department.

text:
This story was originally published on CX Dive. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily CX Dive newsletter.

As Albertsons struggles with its second straight quarter of same-store sales declines, company leaders are turning to better in-store CX and streamlining operations to improve the business.

The grocer has launched a number of initiatives with good reason and intentions, but it has created too many layers of complexity over time, CEO Susan Morris said on a Q2 2026 earnings call Tuesday. Now, Albertsons is turning its focus to a few areas that will create greater value for shoppers.

"We must deliver more consistently for our customers," Morris said on the earnings call. "Price matters, promotions matter, freshness matters, convenience, selection and customer service matter. Our job going forward is to deliver all of those things better than we do today."

Albertsons wants to sharpen its value perception, according to Morris. The amount customers are willing to pay is important, but aspects such as product variety, services and ease of shopping are vital as well.

"Our goal is not to be the cheapest guy in town, but rather to have the right balanced value proposition that resonates with the customers that we serve uniquely by market," Morris said.

Albertsons has its work cut out for it. The grocer's comparable store sales declined just shy of 1% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, according to an earnings report. Digital sales rose 11% year over year, but net sales and other revenue dipped 0.1% year over year to $18.9 billion.

The grocer's plans include strategic price cuts, but it is avoiding broad-based price reductions. Instead, it's making strategic price investments on a more individualized level via tools like the Albertsons for U loyalty program.

"It's about our ability to leverage our very, very strong loyalty program and create personalized offers that may mean something very different to me as a consumer than it might to you as a consumer," Morris said.

Getting the in-store experience right

As Albertsons pursues streamlining its operations, it must "double down on the basics," Morris said. That includes getting the right products inside store formats customers enjoy.

Albertsons stores may be functional, but they fail to offer customers inspiration or excitement, according to Neil Saunders, managing director at GlobalData Retail.

"There's also not nearly enough newness in the offer to showcase new brands and new products," Saunders said in an email. "The whole experience is extremely average, below par even, but when the prices are expensive, that's simply not good enough."

One issue is that Albertsons' stores feel like they "were made for a different era," Saunders said. They tend to be too large for what modern customers expect from a grocer, but Albertsons has let them be rather than invest in reconfiguring the layouts.

Streamlining operations to improve the in-store experience

The grocer's efforts to streamline its store operations and experience plans may include layoffs and closing stores in underperforming markets, according to Morris.

Albertsons has already reduced complexity by cutting the number of regional divisions from 11 to four in July. The change has CX implications, as the regional executive vice presidents who oversee the new divisions were charged with elevating store conditions and keeping store teams focused on taking care of customers, according to Morris.

"With that kind of focus on elevating store standards and execution, it eliminates the distractions from all the noise happening around us," Morris said. "Our team knows that we have essentially two roles in our company: We either serve customers directly or we serve those that serve customers."

Store execution is one of the key areas where Albertsons sees early opportunities for improvement, according to Morris. The company will reduce shrink, raise standards and commit to offering the best training for associates.

"These steps and more, taken together, will improve the customer experience and ultimately our business results," Morris said.
